doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Radio programming integrity and record promoters
summary: Poston tells his hosts not to play music they dislike despite pressure from radio promotion people.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Speaking of that, last question: You’re programming music, it’s your own show and you get a CD in of someone who’s hot and you don’t like it. Do you play it?
I don’t. No. You’re talking about for the radio?

Yeah. The way we handle it, and this is on me because I’m the one who has said this is how we’re going to handle it, our music director gets — I can’t even begin to tell you how many CDs we still get a day.

Yes. A huge amount. They haven’t fully gone to sending files because the digital files still tend to get lost in the mix. But you know there’s a whole — I started to use the word “industry” that’s probably not the right word but there’s a whole industry of radio promotion people that represent artists and labels, that their job is to call the music directors and get them to make sure their artists are played and report the number of spins that that’s getting each week so that it shows up in the jazz Top 40 as, you know, those type things. And there’s a lot of pressure from those kind of things because they’re very good at it, you know they call you certain days that you set it up for them to call and they can convince you that — “Really need your help with this one” to do this or that. I’ve told our music director and I’ve told our hosts as well, don’t ever play anything that you don’t like or that you don’t think is good, I don’t care what it is. We do a pretty good job now of, our music director doesn’t put anything into the library, or doesn’t put tracks in that we don’t feel should be there. So then we’re on a system where everything is digitized. So they have access to the CDs but most of our on-air hosts, they’re pulling stuff up and picking it out from — and what our music director is giving them are approved-of, you know there shouldn’t be anything in there that we’re going to ever be

listening to the radio and think how’d that get played. It happens from time to time obviously. But I’ve told our people, and I believe strongly in it, don’t let outside sources dictate what we play, that — send us the things, if it fits our format and if we think that it fits and if we want to play it we’ll play it, and if not no amount of calling and asking for favors and things is going to work. You know that works to a degree but yeah I mean I don’t believe — now are there exceptions to that? To me no. But I think you treat local artists, you have a little bit more leeway with local artists maybe, just because you know again, you want to support the local jazz scene. Now having said that I mean I can’t think of any local artists that we don’t want to play the things they do, but theoretically you know you would maybe have a little more leeway. But no I think it’s important to maintain your integrity. I’ve always been, with everything I’ve always kind of gone with the idea of maintaining your integrity. I also think though that you should be learned enough, if that’s the right word — I think you should also do all your preparation. I think you should know enough that you could make those kind of decisions because on the same hand too you look — this is all hypothetically — but around the country you may have music directors that just happen to get the job as the jazz music director that doesn’t have the knowledge or the experience or anything like that. Then what do you do? Because again, the idea of, you know, someone being in a position at a radio station to judge whether this is — it’s like a jazz critic I suppose as well. I mean I expect our people to know enough to be able to make a decision. Their decision may not agree with mine, but the person in that music director job I think needs to be knowledgeable enough to make the decisions that the things that go into the library fit our format.
